title: Power of Siberia 2 Back on Putin-Xi Agenda at Bishkek SCO Summit as Modi Courts Central Asia; Iran War Adds $330B to Global Energy Bills
subhead: The SCO's 25th-anniversary summit in Kyrgyzstan brings Russia, China, India and Iran together with the stalled Power of Siberia 2 pipeline on the Putin-Xi bilateral agenda, while new CREA data quantifies the Iran war's $330 billion toll on global energy importers.

sections.heading: Bishkek SCO Summit Puts Power of Siberia 2 Back on the Table
sections.body:
The Kremlin confirmed on Friday that Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold bilateral talks on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, with the long-stalled Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline among the items on the agenda, according to The Diplomatic Insight. Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov called it the second in-person contact between the leaders this year and 'a very important meeting.' The pipeline, which would redirect Russian gas revenues east after the collapse of European markets under sanctions, has remained one of the most consequential unresolved issues in Moscow-Beijing economic relations.

Putin has nine bilateral meetings scheduled over the two-day summit, including with Indian PM Narendra Modi, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The summit, running August 31-September 1, marks 25 years of the SCO and is expected to produce 20-25 documents including a Bishkek Declaration. The leaders will meet again at the BRICS summit in New Delhi in mid-September.
sections.whyItMatters: A Power of Siberia 2 breakthrough would lock Russia's energy future to China for decades and reshape Eurasian gas flows, while the SCO's collective posture on Iran signals a coordinated non-Western bloc position on the Gulf crisis.

sections.heading: Modi's Central Asia Tour: Uranium, Rare Earths and Chabahar Integration
sections.body:
PM Modi's four-day Central Asia visit, which began Saturday, pairs a state visit to Uzbekistan with the Bishkek SCO summit, with energy security and critical minerals at the core of the agenda, per Firstpost. Uzbekistan holds significant reserves of uranium, copper, tungsten and rare earth elements, and long-term uranium supply agreements for Uzbek uranium remain a cornerstone for India's expanding civil nuclear reactor fleet. India is also advocating for full operational integration of the Chabahar Port terminal in Iran into Central Asian transport corridors, alongside the 7,200-km International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) that cuts India-Central Asia transit from 45 days to roughly 20-25 days.

Modi's confirmed bilateral with Putin covers rupee-rouble trade settlement, sustained crude supply contracts, and joint progress on the Kudankulam nuclear power plant. The tour is a direct prologue to India hosting the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13.
sections.whyItMatters: India is using the SCO platform to build an alternative energy and minerals supply chain through Central Asia, reducing dependence on Hormuz-linked routes and Chinese-dominated processing, while positioning itself as a Eurasian power broker ahead of the BRICS summit.

sections.heading: Iran War Added $330 Billion to Global Energy Import Bills
sections.body:
New data from the Finland-based think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates the Iran war added $330 billion to global oil, fuel and LNG import bills between March and August, with crude accounting for $164.1 billion of the total, according to Oilprice.com. Diesel and gasoil added $73.8 billion, gasoline $35.7 billion, and LNG $38 billion. The EU took the biggest hit at $78 billion, followed by China at $35 billion and India at $22 billion.

CREA called the Persian Gulf disruption the biggest since the 1990 Gulf War. The pain is set to persist: Asian LNG prices have averaged roughly 75% above pre-war expectations and European LNG about 60% higher. The IEA earlier estimated as much as a fifth of Middle East refining capacity — some 9.6 million barrels daily — has been knocked out by hostilities, a fuel squeeze that will likely outlast the war itself.
sections.whyItMatters: The CREA figures put a hard number on the war's economic cost and show the burden is falling hardest on import-dependent economies, not the belligerents — a dynamic that will shape winter politics in Europe and Asia.

sections.heading: Venezuela Deal Details Emerge: 25-Year Term, 1.5M bpd Target, OPEC Exit Weighed
sections.body:
Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said the US energy agreement will run 25 years and target crude output of more than 1.5 million barrels per day across 17 strategic oilfields, per Reuters. She said the deal could generate about $209 billion in revenue for the Venezuelan state at a $65-per-barrel benchmark, with roughly $19 per barrel flowing directly to Caracas. Trump on Friday announced the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves through a new company with an unnamed private operator, giving Washington 55% of effective output including rights to buy oil at cost, per AP.

Separately, Rigzone reports Venezuela is weighing an exit from OPEC, the cartel it co-founded in 1960. Chevron is among companies expected to finalize talks to transition its Venezuelan joint ventures into the new framework. Critics, including Harvard's Ricardo Hausmann, called the deal 'shameful' and legally illegitimate, while US gas prices stood at about $4.08 a gallon, up from $3.20 a year earlier.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal's concrete terms — 25 years, 1.5M bpd, a 55% US output share — and the OPEC exit question would, if realized, fundamentally reorder the Western Hemisphere oil map and further erode OPEC's cohesion at a moment of Gulf disruption.

sections.heading: UK Takes Rights to Half of Devon Tungsten Output in £71M State Bet
sections.body:
The UK's National Wealth Fund is investing up to £71 million in Tungsten West to restart the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon, Europe's largest tungsten deposit, according to the Financial Times and The Times via Finanznachrichten. The state receives a roughly 7.4% equity stake and, more significantly, rights to up to 50% of the mine's annual tungsten production. The mine is slated to reach full production in 2027.

The move reflects a broader Western scramble for non-Chinese tungsten: Almonty's Sangdong mine in South Korea has seen its offtake agreement with the Plansee Group extended to 21 years, while the US and Canada have committed $15 million and C$8.2 million respectively to the Sisson tungsten-molybdenum project in New Brunswick. Almonty reported Q2 2026 revenue of about C$43 million, up 498% year-on-year, with European APT tungsten prices at $3,075 per MTU versus $453 a year earlier.
sections.whyItMatters: Governments are moving from subsidy programs to directly securing future output of critical minerals — a state-capitalist turn in Western supply security that signals tungsten, like rare earths, is becoming a strategic commodity rather than a market one.

sections.heading: India's Argentina Minerals Push Goes Beyond Lithium
sections.body:
India's state-owned Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL) is deepening its Argentine footprint, with the fourth India-Argentina Joint Trade Committee meeting in Buenos Aires on August 24 reviewing progress on lithium blocks in Catamarca and exploring expansion into Salta and Jujuy provinces, per ETV Bharat. KABIL's Catamarca venture — the first lithium mining initiative by an Indian company in Argentina — has completed Phase II drilling, but a parliamentary committee flagged 'limited progress' and pushed expected first production back to December 2030.

The broader ambition extends to copper and rare earth elements, with Argentina's government expecting lithium and copper to drive mining exports over the coming decade. Expert Ash Narain Roy told ETV Bharat the engagement signals India moving beyond buying minerals to participating in extraction, a direct challenge to China's dominance of the region's strategic minerals.
sections.whyItMatters: India is trying to build a vertically integrated lithium-to-battery supply chain outside Chinese control, but execution delays show how hard it is to convert overseas mineral rights into actual production — a cautionary counterpoint to the US and UK state-backed pushes.

sections.heading: Hormuz Update: Iran Admits Sanctions Bite as Transit Stays Subdued
sections.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged US sanctions are significantly hurting the economy, telling state television that imports and exports had fallen 25-35% in recent months, per Gulf News. 'We are in a war situation, and we must accept these wartime conditions,' he said, while raising the prospect of higher petrol prices. The Revolutionary Guards navy reiterated Tehran has 'full control' of the strait and rejected US claims it is open.

Shipping through Hormuz remains well below normal: vessel-tracking showed only seven commodity ships transiting on Thursday versus 17 the previous day and a recent daily average of 15, against roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG pre-war. CENTCOM said it had redirected 82 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two as of August 28. Diplomatic efforts led by Qatar, Oman and Pakistan have intensified, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying 'putting diplomacy back on track isn't impossible' if Washington abandons its pressure campaign.
sections.whyItMatters: Tehran's public admission of economic pain is a notable shift after months of downplaying sanctions, and combined with the CREA import-bill data, it raises the pressure on both sides to find a negotiated reopening of the strait before winter.

bottomLine: Today's developments center on the Eurasian energy realignment taking shape at the Bishkek SCO summit, where Power of Siberia 2 is back on the Putin-Xi agenda and India is courting Central Asia for uranium, rare earths and alternative transit routes. Meanwhile, CREA's $330 billion import-bill estimate quantifies the Iran war's economic toll on importers, and the Venezuela deal's concrete terms — 25 years, 1.5M bpd, a 55% US share — plus a possible OPEC exit would reshape the Western Hemisphere oil map. The common thread: states are moving from market reliance to direct, state-backed control of energy and critical mineral supply chains, from UK tungsten to Indian lithium to Russian gas pipelines.
sources: The Diplomatic Insight, Firstpost, Oilprice.com/CREA, Reuters via US News, AP via US News, Rigzone, Finanznachrichten (FT, The Times, Almonty), ETV Bharat, Gulf News
